name: Tamarind
summary: How Filipino growers plant sampalok, the sour kind for sinigang and candy and the sweet kind eaten fresh, either from seed the old way or from grafted seedlings that bear much sooner. It is a tough, long lived tree for dry corners, field edges, dikes and backyards.
season: Trees are planted as the rains begin, about May to June. Grafting and budding are done in the cool dry months, about November to January. Trees flower in the rainy months. Green pods for cooking are picked as they fill, and the ripe brown pods come mostly in the dry months early in the year.
material: Most old trees grew from seed, but seedlings do not come true: the fruit may be sour or sweet, small or big, and the tree takes many years to bear. Seeds from big, well filled pods are washed and soaked in water overnight before sowing. For sweet tamarind or a known sour type, farmers buy cleft grafted or budded seedlings from a nursery.
spacing: Grafted trees about 8 to 10 m apart each way, about 100 to 150 trees a hectare. Seedling trees grow bigger and are planted farther apart, or alone along dikes, roads and boundaries. One seedling a hole.
water: Rain fed. Young trees are watered once or twice a week in their first dry season. After that sampalok stands long droughts and bears with no watering at all.
fertilizer: Rotted manure and compost at planting. Farmers who buy fertilizer give about 100 to 200 g of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) a tree a month after planting and again at the end of the rains, then about 500 g twice a year once bearing, up to 2 kg a year on a big tree. Many trees get nothing and still bear.
care: Ring weeding and mulch while young, watering only in the first dry season, shaping the tree to three or four main branches, removing rootstock shoots on grafted trees, and pruning after the harvest. Fallen, bored pods are gathered and buried.
harvest: Green pods are picked for sinigang as soon as they fill. Ripe pods are picked when the shell is brown, brittle and loose and the pulp sticky. Sweet types are also sold half ripe. Bunches are clipped, not shaken down, so the pods do not crack, then sun dried on mats and kept dry in sacks or jars.

ways.label: Grafted seedlings (punla na grafted)

steps.title: Cleft graft your own seedlings
steps.how: Seedling tamarind does not come true, so growers who want a known sweet or sour type graft a shoot of that tree onto their own tamarind seedlings. Cleft grafting and budding are both used here.

parts.title: Raise the rootstock
parts.how: Soak seeds of any healthy tamarind overnight and sow them in bags. They come up in about two weeks. Grow them on until the stem is about as thick as the shoots you will graft.

parts.title: Graft in the cool, dry months
parts.how: Grafts take best from about November to January, when the weather is cool and dry.

parts.title: Cut scions from the tree you want
parts.how: Early in the morning, cut healthy shoot tips from the sweet or sour tree you want to copy. Strip their leaves without hurting the buds and keep them shaded and moist until grafting, the same day.

parts.title: Split, fit and tie
parts.how: Cut off the seedling top where the stem is still growing, split it down the middle about 2 to 3 cm, and push in the scion cut to a short wedge so the bark lines up. Bind the joint and the scion with a strip of thin plastic and cover the top with a small plastic bag.

parts.title: Care for the new graft
parts.how: Rub off shoots that grow below the joint. When new leaves come from the scion, remove the bag and unwind the plastic, and move the plant to a bigger bag if needed. Plant it out at the start of the rains, about May to June.

steps.title: Dig the holes far apart
steps.how: Pick a sunny spot where water drains, and dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep about 8 to 10 m apart. Mix the topsoil with rotted manure or compost and fill it back.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: On a cloudy day, water the bag, cut it off, and set the seedling at the same depth it grew with the graft joint above the soil. Firm the soil, water, and tie the plant to a stake.

steps.title: Mulch the base
steps.how: Spread dry grass or leaves around the seedling, not against the stem, to keep the soil damp.

steps.title: First feed
steps.how: A month after planting, scatter about 100 to 200 g of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) in a ring away from the stem, and give the same again as the rains end. Manure or compost works too.

steps.title: Remove shoots below the graft
steps.how: Rub off any shoot that grows from the rootstock below the graft joint, and weed a ring under the tree every month or two.

steps.title: Water through the first dry season
steps.how: Water once or twice a week when the rains stop, until the young tree has passed its first dry season. Older trees need no watering.

steps.title: Shape a low, open tree
steps.how: Cut the tip to make it branch and keep three or four well spaced main branches. Remove low, crossing and crowded branches so light gets in and the pods are easy to reach.

steps.title: Watch the pods for borers
steps.how: Once the tree flowers and sets pods, look for holes and frass on the pods from borers and weevils, and pick up and bury fallen damaged pods.

steps.title: Pick the pods
steps.how: Grafted trees bear at about three to four years. Pick green, firm pods for sinigang as they fill. For ripe sampalok, wait until the shell turns brown, brittle and loose and the pulp turns sticky and brown, then clip the bunches so the pods do not crack.
steps.tip: Sweet types are also picked half ripe, when the skin peels easily and the pulp is still crisp.

steps.title: Dry and store the ripe pods
steps.how: Spread ripe pods in the sun on mats for a few days, then keep them in clean sacks or jars in a dry place. Pulp for candy is peeled and seeded by hand.

parts.title: Sun dry the pods
parts.how: Spread the ripe brown pods on mats in the sun for a few days, turning them, and bring them in at night or when rain comes.

parts.title: Shell them by hand
parts.how: Crack and peel off the brittle shell, then pull away the tough strings that run along the pulp.

parts.title: Take out the seeds for candy
parts.how: For sweets and paste, open the pulp and pick out the hard seeds by hand. Keep the best seed for sowing if you want more trees.

parts.title: Pack it clean
parts.how: Pack the cleaned pulp in clean plastic containers or jars and keep it in a cool, dry place. Ripe pulp sells by weight.

steps.title: Prune and feed after harvest
steps.how: After the ripe pods are in, cut out dead, crowded and crossing branches, and give manure plus about 500 g of ammonium sulfate or complete fertilizer twice a year, more as the tree grows.

ways.note: Grafted trees usually start bearing in three to four years, some as early as two. We count the first harvest at 48 months (1,440 days).

ways.label: From seed (punla mula sa buto)

steps.title: Soak and sow the seeds
steps.how: Wash the seeds of big, well filled pods and soak them in water overnight. Sow them about 2 cm deep in bags of garden soil and compost and keep them moist. They come up in one to two weeks.

steps.title: Keep one strong seedling
steps.how: Leave the strongest seedling in each bag and keep the bags weeded and watered.

steps.title: Dig the holes
steps.how: Dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep in a sunny, well drained place, far from houses, and mix the topsoil with manure.

steps.title: Plant at the start of the rains
steps.how: Set out seedlings that have grown in the bag for up to a year, at the same depth. Firm the soil, water and mulch.

steps.title: Feed and weed
steps.how: Give a small amount of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) or manure a month after planting and at the end of the rains, and keep a clean ring under the tree.

steps.title: Shape the young tree
steps.how: Cut the tip to make it branch and keep three or four main branches.

steps.title: Pick the first pods
steps.how: Seedling trees bear from about five years, often later. Taste the first pods. A tree with poor fruit can be top worked with grafts of a good sweet or sour type.

ways.note: Seedling trees stay young and fruitless for five years or longer. We count the first harvest at 72 months (2,160 days).

mistakes: Planting seed from unknown pods and waiting many years for small or poor fruit.
Planting too close to houses, wells or other trees.
Shaking or beating the branches to drop pods, which cracks them and breaks the twigs.
Storing ripe pods damp, so they mold and draw weevils.
Never pruning, so the tree grows tall and dense and bears less.
better: Plant grafted or budded seedlings of a known sweet or sour type for fruit in three to four years.
Top work old poor trees with grafts of a good type.
Prune after harvest to open the tree. Experienced growers also girdle branches before flowering, but learn it from them first.
Test the soil and feed by the result, twice a year.
Scout for pod borers and weevils, clean up fallen pods, and use integrated pest management.

watering.traditional: Sampalok here is rain fed: young trees get a pail of water once or twice a week in their first dry season, and after that the tree is never watered. It stands long droughts on its deep, wide roots and bears with no watering at all.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a ring basin for young trees in their first dry season. Grown trees get rain only. Water in the cool early morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: Plant in May or June as the rains begin, in a sunny, well drained spot, and keep a mulch of dry grass on the ring through the first dry season. After that tamarind needs no watering: it does well both where rain is spread through the year and in places with a long, harsh dry season, thanks to its deep, wide roots.
watering.dryseason: First dry season: once or twice a week, a deep soak of the mulched ring. Older trees: none. Water a young tree when its leaves droop in the afternoon and stay limp by evening, or when it drops leaves early.
watering.wet: Tamarind needs soil that drains and does not like long wet spells. In very wet places it grows leaves but hardly flowers, and rain at the end of pod ripening spoils the pods, so pick ripe pods promptly and dry them on mats under cover.

schedule.stage: Seedlings in bags, for trees raised at home
schedule.often: Every day or two, keeping the bags moist
schedule.amount: Enough to wet each bag through
schedule.why: Soaked seeds come up in one to two weeks and the seedlings must not dry out in the bag.

schedule.often: Water at planting, then only in a dry week
schedule.amount: A good soak of the mulched ring around the stem
schedule.why: Planting with the rains lets the rain carry the young tree.

schedule.often: Once or twice a week once the rains stop, until the dry season ends
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the mulched ring
schedule.why: With enough water a young tree grows about 60 cm in its first year.

schedule.often: No watering needed. Trees from seed stay at this stage until about year 5 or later
schedule.why: The roots spread deep and wide and carry the tree through dry months.

schedule.stage: Flowering and pod set (in the rainy months)
schedule.often: Rain does the work. No watering
schedule.why: Tamarind flowers on the new shoots that come with the rains.

schedule.often: No watering in a normal year
schedule.why: The pods fill on stored soil water as the dry season sets in.

schedule.stage: Ripening and harvest (in the dry months)
schedule.why: Pods lose water as they ripen, and wet weather at the end spoils them.

critical: Seedlings in the nursery bags, which must not dry out.
The first dry season after planting, the only time a tamarind tree needs carried water.

signs.dry: On a young tree, leaves droop in the afternoon, turn yellow and fall early, and new shoots stop.
signs.wet: Yellow leaves and slow growth on soggy ground, and ripe pods that crack or mold in rainy weather.

better: Water young trees faithfully once or twice a week through their first dry season and keep them weeded. With enough water a young tree reaches about 120 cm by its second year.
Never water a bearing tree while its pods ripen. Dry weather then gives the best pulp.
